requirement_groups.name: Core Courses
requirement_groups.source_instruction: The Major in Behavioral Economics Peter Schwardmann, Faculty Director Location: Porter Hall 319F schwardmann@andrew.cmu.edu Lizzy Stoyle, Senior Academic Advisor Location: Porter Hall 208G estoyle@andrew.cmu.edu Schedule an appointment: https://go.oncehub.com/LizzyStoyle https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/undergraduate/behavioral-economics/index.html Overview Behavioral economics has transformed how researchers, businesses, and governments understand human behavior. Rather than assuming that people always make rational decisions , behavioral economists discover how people actually think, choose, and respond to incentives, using scientific evidence to improve products, digital platforms, organizations, markets, and public policy. Today, behavioral economics is becoming central to how organizations understand and improve the decisions of customers, employees, investors, patients, and citizens. Carnegie Mellon offers the nation’s first bachelor’s degree in Behavioral Economics and one of the world’s most comprehensive undergraduate programs in the field. Students learn to think like behavioral economists. Guided by faculty whose research continues to advance behavioral economics, students develop the skills to conduct behavioral research themselves. They design laboratory and field experiments, analyze data, identify causal relationships, evaluate behavioral interventions, and communicate evidence-based recommendations for solving important real-world problems. The major combines rigorous scientific training with quantitative methods, experimental research, and extensive opportunities to apply behavioral economics through research and hands-on projects. Students learn to ask the questions behavioral economists ask, explain why people behave as they do, distinguish causation from correlation, rigorously evaluate competing explanations, and develop practical solutions to behavioral challenges facing organizations, markets, and public policy. The major culminates in a capstone project in which students work as behavioral economists to solve a real-world problem, integrating the scientific , analytical, and practical skills they have developed throughout the program. Organizations increasingly recognize that understanding human behavior is a competitive advantage, and demand for behavioral economists continues to grow. Graduates are well prepared for careers in behavioral science , consulting, product strategy, people analytics, finance, user research, public policy, and many other fields, as well as for graduate study in economics, business, psychology, and related disciplines. Prerequisites All Behavioral Economics majors must complete mathematics and statistics prerequisites (see below), by the end of the sophomore year. Mathematics Prerequisite Units 21-111 & 21-112 Differential Calculus and Integral Calculus 10-20 or 21-120 Differential and Integral Calculus Statistics Prerequisite Units 36-200 Reasoning with Data 9 Curriculum Core Courses The core curriculum in Behavioral Economics consists of three Behavioral Economics courses, two Economic courses, two Psychology courses, three quantitative courses, and one project course. Some courses have additional prerequisites. Behavioral Economics Courses Units 88-360 Behavioral Economics 9 88-365 Behavioral Economics and Public Policy 9 88-367 Designing Economics Experiments in the Wild 9 27 Economics Courses Units 73-102 Principles of Microeconomics 9 or 73-104 Principles of Microeconomics Accelerated Second-Level Economics Course* 88-221 Markets, Democracy, and Public Policy 9 or 88-338 Market Design or 73-103 Principles of Macroeconomics or 73-155 Models, Math, and Markets or 73-230 Intermediate Microeconomics or 73-328 Health Economics or 73-347 Game Theory Applications for Economics and Business or 73-359 Benefit-Cost Analysis or 73-408 Law and Economics or 73-421 Emerging Markets or 73-427 Sustainability, Energy, and Environmental Economics 18 * Second-Level Economics course CANNOT double count with the Economics Elective course. Psychology Courses* Units 88-120 Reason, Passion and Cognition ** 9 88-130 Behavioral Economics for Life 9 or 88-302 Behavioral Decision Making 18 * Students can elect to take 88-120 Reason, Passion and Cognition & 88-130 Behavioral Economics for Life OR 88-120 Reason, Passion and Cognition & 88-302 Behavioral Decision Making Behavioral Decision Making. PLEASE NOTE: Students who have completed 88-302 Behavioral Decision Making OR 88-360 Behavioral Economics cannot take 88-130 Behavioral Economics for Life ** 88-120 Should be taken in the first or sophomore year.
